opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most useful historical examples for thinking about why ordinary people have had any bargaining power at all. The story, roughly, is that Prussia didn't build mass public education out of some pure Enlightenment commitment to human flourishing. It did it in large part because it was competing militarily with its neighbors, and it turned out that a literate, numerate, reasonably healthy population made for better soldiers, better officers, and a stronger industrial base to supply the army. And once Prussia did it and it worked, other states more or less had to follow, or fall behind.

What I take from that is that a lot of what we think of as the moral progress of the modern era, things like universal education, public health, even the gradual extension of the franchise, was at least partly underwritten by the fact that states *needed* their people. Human labor and human fighting capacity were the main sources of national power, so there was a hard-nosed incentive to invest in citizens and keep them reasonably on side. Values and institutions then grew up around that, and I don't want to dismiss those, but I think the material incentive was doing a lot of quiet work underneath.

And that's exactly why it worries me when I think about advanced AI. If you get to a point where AI systems can do most of the economically and militarily valuable work better and more cheaply than humans, then that incentive just evaporates. A state competing with other states no longer gains much by educating, feeding, or empowering its population, because the population isn't where the power comes from anymore. The same competitive pressure that pushed Prussia to invest in people could push future states, or firms, to invest in compute and automation instead, and to treat human welfare as a cost rather than an asset.

So the lesson isn't "competition is good for humans." It's that competition was good for humans *contingently*, because humans happened to be the essential input. That's the sort of thing I mean when I talk about gradual disempowerment. You don't need anyone to be malicious. You just need the background conditions that kept institutions aligned with human interests to quietly stop holding, and then the normal dynamics of competition carry you somewhere none of us would have chosen.

r001.rationale: The response links military competition to education and better soldiers, but does not identify education as necessary for fielding more competitive musket armies.

r002.rationale: It says states had incentives to invest in citizens and keep them on side, but does not state that military competition compelled elites to accept greater citizen empowerment against their preferences.

r003.rationale: It says competition that once incentivized investment in people could instead push states to invest in compute and automation, treating human welfare as a cost. This clearly suggests competitive pressures could reverse citizen-empowering development.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I find that example really striking, and a bit unsettling. So Allan's point, as I understand it, is that Prussia didn't set up mass public schooling primarily because the rulers had suddenly become benevolent. They did it because they'd been humiliated militarily, by Napoleon, and they realized that if you want to compete you need literate soldiers, competent officers, an administrative class, a tax base that can support all of that. And the humane-looking outcome, an educated population, falls out of the competitive pressure almost as a side effect.

And you see that pattern repeated throughout history. States extended the franchise, built welfare systems, improved public health, partly because they needed healthy, motivated, cooperative populations. The people were load-bearing. If you wanted to be powerful, you had to invest in your citizens, and you had to give them some stake in the system, because otherwise they wouldn't fight for you, or work for you, or pay for you.

So the thing I take from it, and the reason I keep coming back to it, is that it tells you what the mechanism was. A lot of the good things we attribute to moral progress were actually underwritten by the fact that ordinary humans were useful. Our leverage came from being needed.

And that's exactly what I worry is changing with AI. If a state, or a company, can get its soldiers and its analysts and its administrators from machines, then the Prussian logic runs in reverse. Competitive pressure no longer pushes you toward educating and empowering your population. It might push you toward sidelining them, because they're a cost rather than an asset. Nothing in the dynamics needs to be malicious for that to happen. It's just that the incentive that was quietly doing a lot of the work disappears.

So I don't read Allan's story as reassuring, like "competition has historically been good for people, so it'll be fine." I read it as a warning about how contingent the good outcomes were. The question we should be asking is: what replaces that mechanism once humans aren't the thing that makes a society competitive?

r001.rationale: It says Prussia needed literate soldiers and other capable personnel to compete militarily, conveying that education supported a more competitive army.

r002.rationale: It explains that rulers invested in citizens and gave them a stake in the system because military and state competition made citizens useful, rather than from benevolence.

r003.rationale: It says competitive pressure could run in reverse, ceasing to push education and empowerment and instead encouraging citizens to be sidelined.

astra-6.text:
The lesson I take from that is that competition can push states to make people more capable, even when the people running those states aren’t particularly interested in their citizens’ welfare. If you need educated people to have an effective army and a productive economy, then you have a reason to invest in education.

But that raises a worrying question about AI: what happens if that connection breaks? If a state can get economic output and military power from machines, then investing in its citizens might become less important to maintaining its power. That doesn’t mean governments will necessarily stop caring about people. It means we could lose one of the pressures that has made caring about people advantageous, even for rulers who weren’t otherwise inclined to do so.

r001.rationale: It links education to an effective army, but does not mention Prussia, musket armies, or their competitive advantage.

r002.rationale: It says competition can motivate state investment in education despite rulers’ limited concern for welfare, but does not state that Prussian elites accepted greater citizen empowerment against their preferences.

r003.rationale: It raises the possibility that AI could weaken incentives to invest in citizens, but does not suggest competitive pressures could reverse the development of citizen-empowering states.

sol-6.1.text:
I take it as a warning about the difference between getting an outcome we like and getting it for reasons that will keep producing outcomes we like. Educating people sounds like progress, but in that account, the pressure was to make the state more effective at military competition. The benefits to citizens were, in some sense, incidental.

And that makes me nervous about relying on competition to make AI go well. Competition can push you to build more capable systems, but it doesn’t necessarily push you to preserve human control or make people better off. If those things stop being useful for winning, the competitive pressure can push against them.

r001.rationale: It says education made the state more effective at military competition, but does not connect citizens’ education specifically to fielding more competitive musket armies.

r002.rationale: It describes pressure to strengthen the state and incidental benefits to citizens, but does not say Prussian elites accepted greater citizen empowerment against their preferences.

r003.rationale: It warns that competition can work against human control or public welfare when those cease to help win, conveying that competitive pressures could reverse citizen-empowering outcomes.
